slides.title: Meet the two tools: TypeSafe Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API
slides.brief: Two cards side by side, one per tool, so a beginner meets both before using them. Left: Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe (San Francisco), launched 15 September 2026. You send text plus questions with fixed options; you get a probability for each option, never a sentence. Reads text only. Example: a support ticket, 'Which team should take it?' returns, shipping or billing. Right: the Decisions API, a service from OpenAI (the company that makes ChatGPT), public beta released 6 October 2026. Same idea: questions with fixed options in, a probability for each option out. Reads text and photos. Example: an egg photo, 'Does the shell look cracked?'. Under both: both run on the company's computers; your program calls them over the internet through an API. No measured numbers on this slide.

slides.title: How to read the numbers in this course
slides.brief: Every number in the course is marked as one of two kinds: the company's own claim from a page you can open, or the presenter's own measurement. One real example answer, 0.99, a probability instead of a sentence.

slides.title: The finish-the-sentence game
slides.brief: An everyday picture: a friend says 'The cat sat on the...' and you say 'mat'. A language model plays the same game with text.

slides.title: Text is cut into tokens, and you pay per token
slides.brief: One sentence cut into small pieces called tokens, with input tokens going in and output tokens coming out, each priced per million.

slides.title: A chat model writes one token, then the next
slides.brief: The model writes token one, reads everything again, writes token two, and so on in a loop, so a longer answer takes more steps in order.

slides.title: Chat models and reasoning models
slides.brief: Compare a chat model that answers directly with a reasoning model that writes hidden thinking tokens first: better on hard problems, but slower and more expensive.

slides.title: A clever clerk, and a cash register that only takes yes or no
slides.brief: A human moment: a shop owner asks a clerk 'is this customer angry, yes or no?' and the clerk answers with a long unsure sentence the cash register cannot read.

slides.title: Four problems when software asks a chat model small questions
slides.brief: Four separate problems side by side: wrong answer shape, slow, costs more than the decision is worth, and no honest signal of doubt.

slides.title: Just ask for JSON? It still has to be parsed
slides.brief: The common belief that asking a chat model for JSON solves everything, shown and then corrected: text still has to be read by code, and a fourth team name or an extra sentence breaks it.

slides.title: Right 95 times in 100, but which 5?
slides.brief: Without a doubt signal a person checks all 100 answers. With an honest doubt signal a person checks only the few flagged ones. The same 100 answers, before and after.

slides.title: The smart if-statement
slides.brief: Normal code branches on simple values like amount > 1000. A smart if-statement branches on common sense, like 'is this email angry?', and the answer goes straight into the code path.

slides.title: Fixed options and probabilities, and two tools that work this way
slides.brief: A chatbot's sentence next to fixed options with a probability for each, for a decision inside code. Four plain gains on the fixed-options side: no text to parse, the answer is always one of your options, a number you can set a cut-off on, and you pay only for what it reads because it writes no text. One everyday example on a line from 0 to 1: 'Is this review spam?' with hide above 0.9, show below 0.1, and a person in the middle. Underneath, the two tools that work this way, each with its logo and date: Jev from TypeSafe, launched 15 September 2026; OpenAI's Decisions API, public beta, released 6 October 2026. If the slide shows OpenAI's speed line, it must be marked as OpenAI's claim: 'OpenAI says about 10x faster than its Responses API'.

slides.title: OpenAI's Decisions API
slides.brief: What the Decisions API does, as a drawing: material (text, a photo, or both) and typed questions go in to the endpoint POST /v1/decisions, a probability for every allowed answer comes out, and no text is written. Facts around the drawing, each from the guide or changelog: released in public beta on 6 October 2026 (O22, O3); one model, gpt-6-luna (O3); price $0.10 per million input tokens, output not billed (O18). One line, clearly marked as OpenAI's claim: 'OpenAI says about 10x faster than its Responses API' (O1, O2). A small note: Jev reads text only (T2), the Decisions API reads text and photos (O1).

slides.title: When to use it, and when not
slides.brief: Two columns. Use the Decisions API when the answer is one of three kinds: is this true (predicate), which option (choice), how much on ordered levels (score), with one everyday example each: is this photo damaged, which team gets this ticket, how bad is this bug (O6). Use the Responses API instead when the model must write something: Structured Outputs for your own JSON layout, such as fields copied out of a document or a written explanation; function calling when a model must request a tool call (O8).

slides.title: The same three question types as Jev
slides.brief: A side-by-side table with three rows. Jev's Noul matches the Decisions API's predicate: one probability from 0 to 1 that a statement is true. Jev's Choice matches choice: one option from your list, with a probability for every option and a confidence. Jev's Score matches score: ordered levels, a score that is the probability-weighted average of the level numbers (O6). Under the table, the guide's rule in one line: no order, like departments, use choice; an order, like severity, use score (O7). One more row at the bottom: Jev reads text only (T2); the Decisions API reads text and images (O1).

slides.brief: A real terminal capture of python 01_first_call_httpx.py from the fresh clone (log 102), with short labels pointing at the parts of the JSON: model gpt-6-luna; answers is a list with one answer per question, each carrying its name 'department'; choice billing; probabilities billing 1.0, technical 0.0, shipping 0.0, other 0.0; confidence 1.0; usage input_tokens 145 and output_tokens 0. A small side note: Jev returns answers keyed by name (the Jev curl answer in the Part 8 guidebook, log 011), the Decisions API returns a list in question order (API reference, 'You'll get the answers back in the order you asked the questions').

Output tokens 0, so nothing to add (log 103, 'output tokens 0'). In plain words: about one and a half thousandths of one US cent. A small footnote with the guide's caveat: 'Regional processing premiums and long-context input pricing multipliers apply' (O19).

The third, 'Which illness does the customer have?', comes back as a refusal, and its arrow goes to 'a person', never to a default answer (log 108). The API reference line: 'The model declined to answer this question. Other questions in the same request can still receive answers.' (O20). A small note: the same illness question with an 'other' option was not refused; it answered 'other' 0.97 (working-copy run, refusal probe). Next to it, a contrast box: an error (HTTP 400) fails the whole request, with no answers at all (log 108, Part 2).

slides.title: A photo travels as text
slides.brief: A photo file becomes base64 text, gets the prefix 'data:image/jpeg;base64,' and goes into the input as an input_image part next to an input_text part ('One egg from a grading line.'), then three questions (choice condition, predicate visible_crack, score dirt_level) come back as three answers. Measured for three photos (log 1010): box10-03, data URL 9,107 characters, 494 input tokens, clean 0.75; duck-04, 30,255 characters, 523 tokens, dirty 1.0; broken-02, 57,775 characters, 650 tokens, cracked 1.0. A footnote on the docs: the guide says base64 data URLs only (O9); the API reference also allows public HTTP(S) URLs (O10); this course always sends base64.

slides.title: How sure, egg by egg
slides.brief: One dot per photo on a line from 0 to 1, the probability the egg is not clean (1 minus P(clean), log 121), coloured by my label. Dirty and cracked eggs sit at 0.89 or higher (lowest duck-01 at 0.89). Clean eggs spread from 0.00 (single-02) to 0.48 (box10-10), except tray-06 at 0.56 (clean 0.44, dirty 0.47 in log 121). The guide's rule underneath: 'Use labeled examples from your application to set thresholds ... Choose thresholds based on the cost of false positives and false negatives.' (O17).

slides.title: Choose on one set, check on another
slides.brief: Two steps in order. Step one: choose the cut-offs on one set of labelled photos. Step two: check them on a second labelled set you did not look at while choosing. A clear note beside it: in this lesson the cut-offs were chosen and checked on the same 33 photos (log 122), so the zero mistakes are a demo of the method, not a proof. No numbers other than 33.

slides.title: OpenAI's speed claim, and our small test
slides.brief: At the top, marked as OpenAI's claim: 'OpenAI says about 10x faster than its Responses API' (O1, O2). Below, our own small test on 10 egg photos, one question, from my laptop, two runs. Fresh run (log 125): Decisions API median 306 ms, matched my labels 10/10, $0.0235 per 1,000 photos; gpt-6-luna on the Responses API writing JSON median 1314 ms, 9/10, $0.0198 per 1,000 photos. Working-copy run: Decisions median 208 ms, 10/10, $0.0235 per 1,000; Responses median 1867 ms, 8/10, $0.0198 per 1,000. Shown as paired bars. A clear footer: 'Our small test, 10 photos. Not proof of OpenAI's number.'

slides.title: The refund desk policy
slides.brief: A claim (a customer message and an egg photo) goes into one call with two questions: what the message says is wrong (broken, dirty, late, other) and what the photo shows (clean, dirty, broken, unclear). Then the written policy as a short flow: any question refused, a person checks; the message claims broken or dirty and the photo shows the same problem with probability 0.90 or more, refund automatically; anything else, a person checks. A bold line: the shop never refuses a refund automatically. A small note on why there are two questions: one combined question ('Does the photo clearly show the problem the customer describes?') refunded 2 of 8 and sent clear broken eggs to a person (C01 0.15, C06 0.00; ~/lab-data/jev-decisions-course/logs/11-returns-desk-v1-output.txt).

slides.title: The message pulls the photo answer
slides.brief: Before and after for two claims. C03 (photo box10-03, a clean egg by my label; the message says one egg is cracked): with the message in the same call, the photo answer was broken, P 0.66, sent to a person (log 126); photo asked alone, the answer was clean, P(broken) 0.01 (log 127). C04 (duck-01, a borderline dirty egg): with the message 0.92, refunded automatically (log 126); alone 0.57, sent to a person (log 127). Totals: one call per claim, 5 refunded and 3 to a person, 1.7 s, 3,463 tokens (log 126); photo on its own, 4 refunded and 4 to a person, 3.1 s, 3,479 tokens (log 127). The guide lines underneath: 'Separate different concerns into different questions' (O15) and 'For decisions that depend on an earlier answer, send separate requests.' (O14).

slides.title: OpenAI's lane example
slides.brief: A screen capture of OpenAI's Decisions guide (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions, read 9 October 2026), section 'Select from fixed options', tab 'Driving': the question 'Which lane should the car choose?' with Lane 1 0.03, Lane 2 0.94, Lane 3 0.03 (saved copy videos/research/sources/decisionsapi/decisions-prose.txt lines 900-907). A label on the capture: 'an illustration on OpenAI's page, not a live run'. Beside it, one line: 'Part 14: a real version you can run'. Capture still needed.

slides.title: The rules of the lane race
slides.brief: How one step of the game works, left to right. A top-down three-lane road with a row every 20 metres; a row holds a barrier or a cone in at most two lanes, never all three (race/road.py make_road). The road comes from a seed: seed 7, 60 steps, the same road for every player. The model answers one choice question, lane 1, 2 or 3, and returns three probabilities. Our code decides: top lane at 0.80 or more, drive into it; below 0.80 or a refusal, slow down and stay (race/play.py). Driving into a lane with something at 20 metres is a crash. A threshold bar from 0 to 1 with 0.80 marked and the band below it labelled 'not sure: slow down'. A small note: in this toy, slowing down never crashes, it only costs time.

slides.title: From a picture, the model was rarely sure
slides.brief: The picture player on seed 7 (log 131-race_picture): 60 steps, one drawn picture per step sent to the Decisions API. Result: 48 slow-downs, 11 clean moves, 1 crash. A strip of 60 small cells, one per step, coloured by action (slow down, drive, crash), with step 35 marked. Step 35 close-up: lane 1 0.83, lane 2 0.02, lane 3 0.15, so the car drove into lane 1, which had a cone at 20 metres (lane 2 had a barrier at 20 metres; fresh-clone results/race/mine/picture-seed7.jsonl, blocked_20m [1, 2]). Step 0 as a second example: lane 2 0.79, just under the cut-off, so it slowed down. Footer: 367 input tokens per step, median 337 ms on the fresh run (213 ms on the run saved in the repository, log 137), $0.0367 per 1,000 steps.

slides.title: A video is a stack of pictures
slides.brief: Why and how a video goes to the Decisions API. The API takes text and images only: 'a text string or user messages containing text and images', 'up to 128 images per request'; 'Other message roles, function calls, files, audio, and item references aren't supported'; there is no video type (FACTS O28, O10). A flip-book picture of a video as frames. The steps in order: a video file (race clip: 244 frames, 8 frames per second, 340 by 400 pixels, 245,050 bytes; log 130), the code cuts the frames it needs at the moment a decision is needed (with ffmpeg from the imageio-ffmpeg package), each frame becomes one input_image, oldest first. Two options: one frame (step 10 -> frame_00040) or the last three frames in one request (frame_00038, 39, 40) so motion is visible (log 130).

slides.title: Three frames cost more and did not help
slides.brief: One frame against three frames per request, same clip, same seed 7, 60 steps, cut-off 0.80 (logs 131-race_clip1, 131-race_clip3). One frame: 0 crashes, 47 slow-downs, 13 clean moves, 391 tokens per step, $0.0391 per 1,000 steps. Three frames: 0 crashes, 50 slow-downs, 10 clean moves, 674 tokens per step, $0.0674 per 1,000 steps; 674 / 391 = 1.7 times the cost. Median time about the same (328 and 345 ms on the fresh run; 203 and 222 ms in the repository run, log 137). Why: in this game the danger does not depend on motion, cones and barriers stand still. One line: send more frames only when the answer depends on movement (not tested here).

slides.title: Five players, one road
slides.brief: The race/compare.py table for seed 7, 60 steps, cut-off 0.80 (log 136, fresh run; log 137, the run saved in the repository, gives the same crashes, slow-downs, moves, tokens and cost). Rows: Decisions, road as text: 0 crashes, 21 slow, 39 moves, 222 tokens per step, $0.0222 per 1,000 steps. Jev, road as text: 0, 4, 56, 432, $0.0181. Decisions, one picture: 1, 48, 11, 367, $0.0367. Decisions, 1 video frame: 0, 47, 13, 391, $0.0391. Decisions, 3 video frames: 0, 50, 10, 674, $0.0674. Median ms, fresh run then repository run: text 208 / 201, Jev 305 / 313, picture 337 / 213, 1 frame 328 / 203, 3 frames 345 / 222. Mark the two text rows as the most decisive and the crash in the picture row. Product logos for OpenAI and TypeSafe on the rows.

slides.title: A cut-off lowers the risk, it does not remove it
slides.brief: What the 0.80 cut-off did for the picture player (log 131-race_picture): it turned 48 unsure steps into slow-downs, which in this game never crash. But one answer was confident and wrong: step 35, lane 1 at 0.83, into a cone. A threshold line at 0.80 with the 48 slow-down steps below it and the 12 steps at or above it (11 clean moves, 1 crash). Three lessons underneath, true for this one road: text was far more decisive than pictures (39 and 56 moves against 11); more frames cost more and did not help; keep a safe action for the not-sure band, and plain checks around the model.

slides.title: Fine for a game, not for a car
slides.brief: A time scale. Measured: one cloud call took a median 0.20 to 0.35 seconds from India (logs 136 and 137: text 0.201 to 0.208 s, pictures and frames 0.203 to 0.345 s, Jev 0.305 to 0.313 s). Where that is fine: a turn-based game, a review queue such as the egg grading line in Part 13. Where it is not: a real car's control loop, which cannot wait for an internet call, and a call can be slow or fail. A clear label: 'a toy that teaches pictures, frames and cut-offs, not a driving system'. No car brand, no drawn people.

slides.title: Same tickets, same rules
slides.brief: How Jev and OpenAI's Decisions API were tested on the same job, in order, each tool with its product logo. The same 300 support tickets with the same right answers, and the same three questions word for word: which team, how urgent, how frustrated, all three in one call (FACTS line 85). Five warm-up calls per tool, not counted (line 86). For one call at a time: 40 tickets, three rounds, the two tools take turns and the order swaps each time (line 86). For the whole batch: 300 tickets with 8 calls in flight (line 85). No retries; failed calls and refusals: 0 and 0 in every run (line 104).

slides.title: Three runs on one day
slides.brief: The same test run three times on 9 October 2026 from Kolkata, at 11:25, 12:02 (fresh clone) and 12:06 India time (FACTS lines 82-84), Jev against the Decisions API, each with its product logo. Two rows stay the same every run: team answers right, Decisions 295 of 300 in all three runs, Jev 290, 290, 291 (lines 90-91); cost per 1,000 tickets, Decisions $0.0506 and Jev $0.0246 in all three runs (lines 96-97). One row moves: time for all 300 tickets with 8 calls in flight, Decisions 7.7 s, then 13.3 s, then 13.4 s; Jev 12.5 s, 12.9 s, 12.6 s (lines 98-99). Mark the accuracy and cost rows as repeated and the speed row as not repeated. A footnote: public beta, measured from India, measure speed at your own time and place (lines 108-114). Optional small rows: urgency right, Decisions 239 every run, Jev 217, 217, 216; frustration right, Decisions 239 every run, Jev 226, 227, 226 (lines 92-95).

slides.title: Price per token is not price per ticket
slides.brief: Why Jev's price per token is 2.4 times lower but its cost per ticket is only 2.1 times lower. Price per million input tokens: Decisions $0.10 (FACTS line 33), Jev $0.042 (line 47); 0.10 / 0.042 = 2.4. Cost per 1,000 tickets: $0.0506 against $0.0246 (lines 96-97); 0.0506 / 0.0246 = 2.1. Each call is a parcel: a fixed part (the three questions plus each tool's own wrapping) and the ticket text inside. Fitted fixed part about 466 tokens on Decisions and about 543 on Jev; the ticket text reads at about 4.33 and 4.19 characters per token, about 40 tokens per ticket on both (from compare_decisions/results/summary.md, fresh-run log 204-cd_summarize.txt; these four numbers are not in FACTS). Tokens per ticket in total: Decisions 506, Jev 585 (line 115). The lesson: compare dollars per ticket on your own tickets.

slides.title: The lane race, text only, both tools
slides.brief: Jev and the Decisions API on the same seeded road (seed 7, 60 steps, cut-off 0.80), both reading the road as text, with product logos (log 136; log 137 has the same counts). Decisions: 0 crashes, 21 slow-downs, 39 clean moves, 222 input tokens per step, $0.0222 per 1,000 steps, median 208 ms (201 ms in log 137). Jev: 0 crashes, 4 slow-downs, 56 clean moves, 432 input tokens per step, $0.0181 per 1,000 steps, median 305 ms (313 ms). Two notes: Jev read more tokens but cost less per step, because its price per token is 2.4 times lower ($0.042 against $0.10 per million, FACTS T3 and O18); and 0.80 means a different thing on each tool, so each needs its own cut-off. One road, one seed: a small test.

slides.title: What each one can do
slides.brief: Three columns, with product logos: only the Decisions API, both, only Jev. Both: many independent questions in one call (FACTS line 28 for Decisions; Jev shown in Part 9), a probability for every option, and a confidence number for a choice or a score (line 31). Only the Decisions API: reads photos, text plus images (line 16), and can return a refusal for one question while the others are still answered (line 35). Only Jev: the state can be a JSON object with named fields, like a form (line 46: 'String, JSON object, or array of text values'). Jev reads text only: 'No image, audio, or video input' (line 46).

slides.title: Which tool for which job
slides.brief: A simple choice between three tools. Decisions about text only, many of them, where cost matters: Jev, which cost about half as much on these 300 tickets (FACTS lines 96-97). Decisions about photos, or text with photos: OpenAI's Decisions API, the only one of the two that reads images (lines 16 and 46). Written text for a person, or an answer in your own JSON shape: a chat model with structured output, as OpenAI's own Decisions guide says (line 23). Under all three, one rule: test on your own labelled data, set two cut-offs, and send the unsure middle to a person (line 32). On these tickets the Decisions API was a little more accurate (lines 90-95), so the test on your own data matters.

slides.title: Jev or a chat model?
slides.brief: A simple choice: if the program needs a decision from a fixed list of answers about text, use Jev; if it needs written text for a person, use a chat model. One note: Jev reads text only, so a decision about a photo needs a model that reads images, such as OpenAI's Decisions API.

slides.title: Using both: the cheap check first
slides.brief: A cascade: every request gets a fast, cheap typed check, and only the unclear or hard ones go on to the larger, slower model. Real product logos.

slides.title: Using both: the cheap check first
slides.brief: A cascade, as in Part 6: either Jev (TypeSafe) or the Decisions API (OpenAI) can sit in front, each named in words with its logo, neither shown as the only front tool. High confidence: your code acts. Low confidence: the request moves on, to a larger model or to a person.

slides.title: Five things to remember
slides.brief: Five practical things to remember about using Jev or the Decisions API, on one screen. One: both answer typed questions (yes or no, one option from a list, a level on a scale) with probabilities; ask all questions about the same material in one call, because every call pays a fixed part (FACTS line 28 and line 116: three questions in one call 505 against 594 tokens per ticket on Decisions, 583 against 1,184 on Jev). Two: wording matters on both; write the question you mean, with options that are clearly different (line 30). Three: use the confidence; two cut-offs, the unsure middle to a person, a stricter cut-off for anything that moves money (line 32). Four: log which model answered every call; on Jev, pin jev-1.13.0. Five: test on your own labelled data; tune on one set, check on a set never used for tuning.

slides.title: Keys, errors and refusals
slides.brief: A checklist of what app/app.py does to stay safe. Keys come from .env only (load_env_file, line 34); they are never typed in the code and never shown on the page. One OpenAI client and one Jev client, made once and reused (@st.cache_resource, lines 39-48). Automatic retries off, so each time shown is one real call (max_retries=0, line 42); in a real service keep retries on (FACTS 'Retries'). Every call runs inside safe() (lines 67-73): a failed call shows a red error box and the app keeps working. A refusal shows a yellow warning, 'Send it to a person' (lines 108-109, 147-148, 179-180). The fresh-clone app test showed 0 errors on the page (log 140).

slides.title: The button calls, the slider does not
slides.brief: How Streamlit runs and why a slider never calls the API. Streamlit runs the whole script again, top to bottom, on every click or slider move: a whiteboard wiped and redrawn after every touch. The call sits inside 'if st.button("Ask")', so it runs only on the click that pressed the button (app/app.py line 97). The answer is saved in st.session_state, a notebook beside the whiteboard that is not wiped (line 98). The slider comes after the call (line 105); moving it reruns only the cut-off rule on the saved answer, so ACT or DO NOT ACT changes with no new call and no new cost. Two lanes drawn side by side: a click (call, save, draw) and a slider move (read saved answer, apply cut-off, draw).

slides.title: What one click costs
slides.brief: The cost of each click, from the usage block in each answer times the price (log 140, fresh clone). Predicate, Decisions: 174 input tokens, $0.0000174, 403 ms; Jev on the same message: 292 tokens, $0.00001226, 449 ms. Choice on the tray-06 egg photo, Decisions: 226 tokens, $0.0000226, 384 ms. Score, Decisions: 160 tokens, $0.0000160, 186 ms; Jev: 341 tokens, $0.00001432, 407 ms. Prices: Decisions $0.10 per million input tokens (FACTS O18), Jev $0.042 per million (FACTS T3). Derivation shown for one row: 174 x 0.10 / 1,000,000 = $0.0000174. One line: every click costs less than three thousandths of a US cent.
